act: AIFC Banking Business Prudential Rules (BBR), V6
title: Capital conservation ratios: Table 4A is entered by the CET1 capital ratio, while the buffer under 4.31(2) excludes CET1 used for the T1 and Total Capital ratios
summary: BBR 4.31(2) provides that the capital conservation buffer must be made up of CET1 capital above the amounts used to meet the CET1, T1 and Total Capital ratios, and 4.32(1) requires a bank whose buffer falls below the required minimum to restrict its distributions. Under 4.32(2) and Table 4A, however, the minimum capital conservation ratio is selected by the bank's CET1 capital ratio, which does not exclude the CET1 used to meet the T1 and Total Capital ratios; a ratio above 7% gives 0%. For a bank whose capital is all CET1, the buffer becomes positive only above 8% of risk-weighted assets and reaches 2.5% at 10.5%. With risk-weighted assets of USD 1,000 million, CET1 of USD 85 million (8.5%) and no AT1 or T2 capital, the bank's ratios are above the minima, its buffer under 4.31(2) is USD 5 million against USD 25 million, so it is in breach of 4.31(1) and 4.32(1) requires it to restrict distributions; yet Table 4A sets no positive minimum retention (0%). BPG Chapter 4 paragraph 11(c) states that a bank with a CET1 capital ratio of more than 7% can distribute 100% of its earnings; 4.33(1) also compares CET1 with the CET1 ratio plus the buffer. IBB 5.2 to 5.4 and Table 5.1 have the same structure. Basel III paragraph 131 measures the CET1 ratio of the table excluding the CET1 needed for the 6% Tier 1 and 8% Total Capital requirements.
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

act: AIFC Banking Business Prudential Rules (BBR), V6
title: Significant and non-significant investments: the definition in 4.27, the heading of 4.29(4) and the conditions of 4.29(4)(a) and 4.29(6)(a) classify a holding of AT1 or T2 instruments differently
summary: BBR 4.27 defines a significant investment as an investment of 10% or more in the common shares, or other instruments that qualify as capital, of the entity concerned. The heading of Rule 4.29(4), which is part of the Rules under section 24(1)(a) of the AIFC Regulations on AIFC Acts, describes non-significant investments as those "where the Bank does not own more than 10% of issued common equity of the entity". Rule 4.29(4) then applies where the Bank makes a non-significant investment and does not own more than 10% of the common shares, and Rule 4.29(6) where the Bank makes a significant investment and owns 10% or more of the common shares. A holding of 10% or more of an issue of AT1 or T2 instruments of another bank or insurer, with less than 10% of its common shares, is non-significant by the heading and significant by 4.27, and under the conditions of the two rules it is outside both of them. Take an unconsolidated issuer whose only instrument other than common shares is a T2 issue of USD 300 million, with no reciprocal holding and no pledge: for a bank with CET1 of USD 100 million, a holding of USD 30 million (10% of the issue) with no common shares is not deducted under the conditions of 4.29, while the heading and line 37 of Form 30 lead to a deduction of the excess of USD 20 million; a holding of USD 29.7 million (9.9%) leads to a deduction of USD 19.7 million. The heading also uses "not more than 10%" where 4.27 uses "10% or more".
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

act: AIFC Banking Business Prudential Rules (BBR), V6
title: Maturity mismatch limits: the net cumulative position is inflows less outflows, and 9.21(4) requires it not to exceed negative 15% and negative 25%
summary: BBR 9.21(1)(c) defines the net cumulative maturity mismatch position as inflows (assets) less outflows (liabilities) in each time band, and 9.21(3) expresses it as a percentage of Total Deposits; line 5 of Form 81 in the Manual for Preparation of Returns uses the same sign. Rule 9.21(4) then requires the position not to exceed negative 15% (sight to 8 days) and negative 25% (sight to 1 month), and the Bank must notify the AFSA if it exceeds these limits. Read as written, a bank with Total Deposits of USD 100 million whose inflows up to 8 days are USD 110 million and outflows USD 100 million (a position of +10%) exceeds negative 15% and breaches the limit, while a bank whose inflows are USD 40 million against outflows of USD 100 million (-60%) does not exceed it. The flows are those included in the maturity ladder under the BPG. IBB 10.30(4) and (5) have the same text (the denominator in IBB 10.30(3) also includes UPSIA accounts).
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

act: AIFC Banking Business Prudential Rules (BBR), V6
title: NSFR required stable funding: unencumbered HQLA securities with a residual maturity of one year or more fall within the descriptions of two RSF categories
summary: Under BPG Chapter 9 paragraph 177(a) each asset is assigned to one of the eight RSF categories, and BBR 9.19(2) requires the NSFR to be calculated in accordance with Chapter 9 of the BPG (it refers to Section E; the NSFR methodology is in Section H). Paragraph 179 assigns unencumbered Level 1 HQLA to Category 2 (5%), paragraphs 181 and 182(a) assign Level 2A and 2B HQLA to Categories 4 and 5 (15% and 50%), and paragraph 184(c) assigns 'unencumbered securities with residual maturity of 1 year or more' to Category 7 (85%). Unlike paragraph 184(d) and row 24 of the disclosure template Table 13, paragraph 184(c) does not exclude securities that qualify as HQLA, and no rule sets which description prevails. For a bank with available stable funding of USD 1,000 million, other required stable funding of USD 700 million and an unencumbered five-year Level 1 government bond of USD 500 million, the NSFR is 137.9% under paragraph 179 and 88.9% under paragraph 184(c). Form 201 in the Manual for Preparation of Returns repeats both lines (10.1 and 15.3), and IBB Appendix 1 paragraphs 131 and 136(c) repeat the same overlap (for an Islamic Bank, for example a Level 1 sovereign sukuk).
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

act: AIFC Islamic Banking Business Prudential Rules
title: Accumulated losses already reflected in retained earnings: IBB 4.13 and 4.39
summary: IBB 4.13(c) includes retained earnings in Common Equity Tier 1 capital, and the Guidance to 4.13, which under IBB 1.3(b) is part of the rules, states that retained earnings and other comprehensive income include appropriated profit or loss. IBB 4.13(f) includes the regulatory adjustments under 4.30, which points to 4.31 to 4.45, and IBB 4.39 requires an Islamic Bank to deduct from its CET1 capital the amount of any accumulated losses, without distinguishing losses already reflected in retained earnings. Read as written, a loss of prior years reduces CET1 capital twice: an Islamic Bank with common shares of USD 100 million and retained earnings of minus USD 20 million would report CET1 of USD 60 million, or USD 80 million if 4.39 does not apply to losses already reflected in retained earnings. BBR 4.14(c) and 4.28(11) have the same structure, and BPG Chapter 4 paragraph 7 states the same for BBR 4.14.
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

act: AIFC Islamic Banking Business Prudential Rules
title: Islamic banks — significant and non-significant investments: an investment that is significant under 4.29 through Additional Tier 1 or Tier 2 instruments, with less than 10% of the common shares, is not covered by 4.43 or 4.45
summary: IBB 4.29 defines a significant investment as an investment of 10% or more in the common shares, or other instruments that qualify as capital, of the entity concerned. Rule 4.43 applies where the Islamic Bank makes a non-significant investment and does not own 10% or more of the common shares; Rule 4.45 applies where it makes a significant investment and owns 10% or more of the common shares. An investment that is significant through Additional Tier 1 or Tier 2 instruments, with less than 10% of the common shares, is outside both rules, and no other rule in 4.40 to 4.46 deducts it: 4.42 covers reciprocal cross holdings only, and 4.45(3) and 4.46 cover common shares and other CET 1 instruments only. The headings of 4.43 to 4.45 do not refer to the shareholding. Take an unconsolidated Islamic Bank whose only instrument other than common shares is an issue of Tier 2 sukuk of USD 300 million, with no reciprocal holding and no pledge: for an Islamic Bank with CET 1 Capital of USD 100 million, a holding of USD 30 million (10% of the issue) with no common shares is not deducted, while a holding of USD 29.7 million (9.9%) leads to a deduction of the excess of USD 19.7 million under 4.44.
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

act: AIFC Rules on Digital Asset Activities (DAA), V5
title: Part 4 covers issuers of Commodity stablecoins, but authorisation (4.1) and capital (4.2) name only Fiat stablecoins

The current version keeps this. Rule 4.11.3(1) says "In addition to DAA 4.2(b), an issuer of a Fiat stablecoin or Commodity stablecoin" must hold ongoing capital of 2%, so it assumes that 4.2(b) applies to both. GEN Schedule 1, paragraph 21, Guidance (5) also mentions only Fiat stablecoins. A Commodity-stablecoin issuer might be covered as "Providing Money Services in relation to Digital Assets" (buying and selling of a Digital Asset), but 4.1(2) treats issuing as a separate activity. The rules therefore do not say clearly which licence a Commodity-stablecoin issuer needs or whether the USD 200,000 floor in 4.2(b) applies to it.

act: AIFC Rules on Digital Asset Activities (DAA), V5
title: DAA 2.8.2(1)(c): stablecoin admission criteria "in (4) or (5)": (5) is a notice after admission, and the reserve test in (4)(c) covers only Fiat stablecoins
summary: DAA 2.8.2(1)(c) makes admission of a Fiat or Commodity stablecoin to trading depend on "all of the requirements in (4) or (5) as applicable". Paragraph (4) lists reserve criteria, but its test of reserve adequacy in (4)(c) speaks only of "reserves in respect of Fiat stablecoins". Paragraph (5) is not a criterion: it requires the operator to notify the AFSA within 3 business days after admission (in earlier versions, 10 days before admission). So for a Commodity stablecoin the operator has no stated test that the reserves cover the stablecoins in circulation. Issuers licensed in the AIFC must still meet the reserve rules in DAA 4.7.1, which cover Commodity stablecoins, and the AFSA approves stablecoins other than those issued by licensed Digital Asset Service Providers (2.8.1(3)(b)); the gap concerns the operator's admission test, mainly for stablecoins issued outside the AIFC. act: AIFC Rules on Digital Asset Activities (DAA), V5
title: DAA 4.7.2: annual reserve audit may end 4 months after year end, but its result is due 4 weeks after the 'reference date of the valuation'

"Reference date of the valuation" is not defined, and (1) does not say whether the four months apply to commissioning or to completing the audit. If the reference date is the financial-year end, the result could be due before the audit has to be done.

act: AIFC Rules on Digital Asset Activities (DAA), V5

For an issuer with several categories, 4.11.3(3) says this amount "should be the sum of the average amounts of the reserve assets backing each category", and the Guidance describes it as the average amount of reserve assets at the end of each day over the preceding 6 months. Reserve assets must be at least equal to the outstanding stablecoins (4.7.1(2)) and may be larger. For an issuer with one category, the binding text does not say which base applies or over what period the average is taken.

act: AIFC Rules on Providing Money Services (PMS)
title: PMS 4.3 and 7.3(3) list different cases in which a redemption fee may be charged: may a fee be charged for a redemption during the agreement?
summary: Two rules govern fees on the redemption of Electronic Money, and both use "only where". PMS 4.3(1) allows a fee where (a) the redemption is requested before the termination of the client agreement, (b) a fixed-term agreement is terminated early, or (c) redemption is requested more than one year after termination. PMS 7.3(3) allows a fee only where it "relates to early termination or late redemption". A redemption requested at early termination meets both rules. A redemption during a running agreement, without termination, is allowed by 4.3(1)(a) and referred to in 4.4(1), but does not fit 7.3(3). Read together, such a fee is not allowed, which leaves little room for 4.3(1)(a).

act: Rules and mechanisms of cooperation of unbacked digital asset exchanges and Centre Participants with second-tier banks of the Republic of Kazakhstan

act: AIFC Rules on Digital Asset Activities (DAA), V5
title: DAA 4.7: the reserve of a Fiat stablecoin is only operationally segregated; the Rules do not say whether it is protected from the issuer's own creditors and how it is shared among holders on insolvency
summary: DAA 4.7.1(4) requires the issuer of a Fiat stablecoin to ensure that the reserve of assets is "operationally segregated from the proprietary assets of the issuer". DAA 4.7.3(7) requires the custody arrangements to protect the reserve against "claims of the custodian's creditors", and DAA 4.7.3(1)(a) requires that the reserve is "not encumbered nor pledged as Collateral". DAA 4.11.2(1) requires the issuer to grant holders redemption rights "on the reserve assets when the issuer is not able to comply with its obligations", while DAA 4.5(1)(c) speaks of "the rights or the absence of rights granted to the holders". The DAA, PMS and COB do not state that the reserve is held on trust for holders or is otherwise outside the issuer's estate. Under the Insolvency Regulations (Schedule 3) property of a company excludes only property held on trust, and under rule 5.46.1 of the Insolvency Rules unsecured debts rank equally. Because the issuer is a Money Service Provider (DAA 4.1(1)), COB 8.2 applies to it (COB 8.1.4), and COB 8.2.16(2)(c) requires money remaining with the firm to be paid to each Client before the general order of winding up; it is not clear whether this covers the reserve, which is not Client Money under COB 8.2.1 and PMS 9.3, and holders who have no client agreement with the issuer (DAA 4.11.2(3)). DAA 4.7.2(3)(b) refers to an issuer "required to implement a redemption plan", but no rule sets out such a plan. Example: if the reserve forms part of the estate and holders rank as unsecured creditors, an issuer with 50 million USD of coins in circulation, a reserve of 50 million USD, no other assets, other unsecured creditors of 10 million USD and winding-up costs of 1 million USD pays holders about 82 cents per coin (49 / 60). The wording of 4.7.1(4), 4.7.3(7) and 4.11.2(1) is close to Articles 36(3), 37 and 39(1) of the EU Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (EU) 2023/1114; Article 36(2) of that Regulation, which requires the reserve to be legally segregated from the issuer's estate so that the issuer's creditors have no recourse to it, has no counterpart in the DAA.
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

location: Glossary, «Investment Business», p.26 (the exclusion follows the whole list (a)–(k))
title: Unclear application of the Client Money Rules to fiat currency held for Clients in Digital Asset Business
summary: The Glossary defines Investment Business as a list of activities (a) to (k), "but not including Digital Asset Business", and Digital Asset Business includes Operating a Digital Asset Trading Facility and the other activities in relation to Digital Assets. COB 8.1.4 requires compliance with the Client Money Rules (COB 8.2) by a firm that holds Money for a Client "in the course of, or in connection with, the carrying on of Investment Business or Provides Money Services", and COB 8.2.1 defines Client Money by Investment Business. A Digital Asset Trading Facility Operator holds fiat currency for its Clients (DAA 2.13.4(2): a trade only if there are "sufficient Fiat Currencies or Digital Assets … in the Client's account"). Digital Assets of the same Clients "must be held on trust" (DAA 2.13.7(2), 3.7.1(3)), but no rule says the same of their fiat currency. The Rules of cooperation with second-tier banks require a Digital Asset Service Provider to hold Clients' money and its own money in separate accounts (rule 2.2.3), and DAA 2.13.7(7)(a) requires "segregation and portability arrangements". COB chapter 8 is listed among the applicable provisions only in Guidance to DAA chapters 2 and 3. It is therefore unclear whether this fiat currency is Client Money, whether the Client Money Distribution Rules in COB 8.2.16 apply to it if the firm fails (COB 8.1.2(c) brings in chapter 8 for a firm that Provides Custody, but not for a trading facility that uses a third-party wallet provider or for a broker), and whether it is Excluded Property under Schedule 4 of the Insolvency Rules. Example: a client deposits 20,000 USD with a Digital Asset Trading Facility Operator that uses a third-party wallet provider; the money is held in a separate account under rule 2.2.3; if the operator fails with a shortfall in that account, the Rules do not say how the shortfall is shared.
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

act: AIFC Rules on Digital Asset Activities (DAA), V5
title: Capital of Digital Asset Service Providers: DAA Table 2 and PRU (INV) Table 3.3 both apply to the same activities with different amounts
summary: DAA 3.2(1)(b) and Table 2 set the capital of a Digital Asset Service Provider at USD 250,000 for Providing Custody, USD 100,000 for Managing Investments and USD 250,000 for Dealing in Investments as Principal (other than matched principal). PRU (INV) 1.3 applies to any firm authorised to conduct these activities; Investments include Digital Assets (Glossary), and PRU (INV) 1.3(6) does not exclude Digital Asset Business. PRU (INV) Table 3.3 sets USD 500,000 for Providing Custody Services and for Dealing in Investments as Principal and USD 150,000 for Managing Investments, with the liquid assets requirement in PRU (INV) 4. DAA 3.2(1)(a) keeps the general authorisation requirements of other applicable rules, and for stablecoin issuers DAA 4.2(b) states that "the highest amount applies" where another activity requires more capital, so the DAA amounts may be meant as a floor next to PRU (INV). The Rules do not say so for Table 2. Example: a firm licensed only to provide custody of Digital Assets with capital resources of USD 300,000 meets Table 2, but is USD 200,000 below PRU (INV) Table 3.3 for the same activity.
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

location: Companies Regulations V8, s.92(2) unnumbered paragraph
title: Companies Regulations s.92: the consolidated PDFs on aifc.kz make the fine clause refer to itself; Amendments No. 2 and the AFSA online text number it correctly

title: Companies Regulations s.26-1(2)(b): the confirmation statement covers duties "mentioned in subsection (2)", but the duties are listed in (3)
summary: Section 26-1(2)(b) requires a statement that all information required "under any duty mentioned in subsection (2)" has been delivered. Subsection (2) is the provision itself and mentions no duty. The list of duties ("The following duties require notification in Writing:") is subsection (3). Subsection (1) is the election, and the only list of duties follows in (3), so the reference reads as written for a text in which the list was subsection (2). The wording has been the same since Amendments No. 4 (in force 1 January 2020).
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Companies Regulations s.26(1-1)(c): annual return takes director particulars from s.13(4)(j), which is the UBO item; directors are in s.13(4)(h)
summary: s.26(1-1)(c) requires "the particulars mentioned in section 13(4)(j) (Formation of companies) for each Director and, if applicable, the Secretary". s.13(4)(j) is "the particulars required by Part 14-1 (Ultimate Beneficial Owners)". The directors and secretary item is s.13(4)(h): "the full name ..., nationality, address, business occupation (if any) and date of birth of the individuals who are to serve as the Directors and, if applicable, the Secretary". The words "for each Director and, if applicable, the Secretary" fit only (h).
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Companies Regulations s.26(4): the fine clause was not updated when Amendments No. 4 moved the annual-return deadline and contents into a new subsection (1-1)
summary: Amendments No. 4 moved the annual-return deadline and contents from section 26(1) of the Companies Regulations into a new subsection (1-1). Section 26(4) still makes "subsection (1), (2-1) or (3)" punishable by a fine, and item 10 of Schedule 3 of the Companies Rules still says "26(1) or (3)". The reference to (1) may be read as reaching the re-enacted duty (section 21(2) of the AIFC Regulations on AIFC Acts), but a reader of section 26(4) cannot see that late or incomplete filing is finable. Item 10 also does not list subsection (2-1), which section 26(4) makes finable.
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA); AIFC Authority

title: Companies Rules 5.3 (transfer out of the AIFC): since V4 the subrules are numbered 5.3.3-5.3.6, and three cross-references, including the 60-day notice, point to numbers that no longer exist
summary: In the Companies Rules V1-V3, rule 5.3 has 5.3.1 (application, with (c) "a declaration ... under subrule 5.3.3"), 5.3.2, 5.3.3 ("For rule 5.3.1(c), the declaration ... must state") and 5.3.4 (60-day notice before "an application mentioned in subrule 5.3.1"). From V4 (in force 1 January 2020) the same subrules are numbered 5.3.3-5.3.6 and there is no 5.3.1 or 5.3.2, but the text is unchanged. So 5.3.3(c) now points to itself, 5.3.5 points to "5.3.1(c)" and 5.3.6 ties the 60-day notice to "an application mentioned in subrule 5.3.1". The Companies Rules on the AFSA website (read on 24 October 2026) have the same numbering. No published amending act changes rule 5.3. Rule 5.3 deals with one application only, so the meaning can be recovered.
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

title: Companies Regulations ss.179-6(1) and 179-7: after Amendments No. 4 moved the Nominee Director particulars to 179-7(1-1), the references in 179-6(1) and in the fine clause 179-7(2) were not updated
summary: Amendments No. 4 moved the particulars of the Register of Nominee Directors from section 179-7(1) into a new subsection (1-1). Section 179-6(1) still refers to "section 179-7(1)(a) to (e)", and section 179-7(2) still makes only "subsection (1)" finable. Section 21(2) of the AIFC Regulations on AIFC Acts allows both references to be read as reaching the moved list, so this is a matter of clarity rather than a gap.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Companies Rules Schedule 3, items 62 and 64: "179-4(8) or (21)" and "179-7(2) or (15)" name the "in Writing" subsections; the fine clauses of these regimes are 179-4(22) and 179-7(16)
summary: Schedule 3 of the Companies Rules sets fine limits by naming provisions of the Companies Regulations. Items 62 ("179-4(8) or (21)") and 64 ("179-7(2) or (15)") first appear in V4 (in force 1 January 2020); V3 had only "179-4(8)" and "179-7(2)". Subsections 179-4(21) and 179-7(15) only require notices to be "in Writing", while the fine clauses for these regimes are 179-4(22) and 179-7(16). The same change added "52(17)", also a fine clause, to item 18, so (21) and (15) look off by one. No published amending act contains this change. The Companies Rules on the AFSA website (read on 24 October 2026) have the same text. Whether items 62 and 64 set a limit for breaches of 179-4(9)-(20) and 179-7(3)-(14) depends on how the description in column 3 is read.
reported_to: Astana Financial Services Authority (AFSA)

title: Companies Regulations Schedule 1 and NPIO Regulations s.33(5): "Objectives" of the Registrar defined by s.9(1) of the Companies Regulations; the objectives are in s.10(1)
summary: Both definitions point to "section 9(1) (Registrar's Objectives and Functions)". s.9 is "Appointment of Registrar". The objectives are set in s.10(1) ("(the Registrar's Objectives)"), whose heading is the one in brackets. The bracketed heading saves the meaning.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

location: Insolvency Rules V3, rule 9.1, subrule numbered 8.1.1(b)
title: Insolvency Rules, rule 9.1: the consolidated PDFs on aifc.kz number its subrules 8.1.1-8.1.6, while 8.1.1(b) and 9.3.1(a) cite "9.1.3"
summary: Amendments No. 1 to the Insolvency Rules (2 December 2018) inserted rule 9.1 with subrules 9.1.1-9.1.6. The consolidated PDFs on aifc.kz (V2 and the current V3) print them as 8.1.1-8.1.6, while 8.1.1(b) and 9.3.1(a) still cite "9.1.3". The Insolvency Rules on the AFSA website (read on 24 October 2026) number them 9.1.1-9.1.6, so the cited subrule exists there.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Insolvency Regulations s.88(2): the Rules may vary "requirements mentioned in subsection (2)", i.e. in the power itself; the criteria are in (1)
summary: Section 88(1) says the Rules must prescribe the criteria for registration as an insolvency practitioner or official liquidator. Section 88(2) lets the Rules vary "requirements mentioned in subsection (2)" for applicants regulated outside the AIFC. Subsection (2) is the power itself and mentions no requirements; the criteria are in (1). The parallel provision for auditors, section 134(3) of the Companies Regulations, refers to the subsection that sets the criteria.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Insolvency Regulations ss.98-99: where inability to pay is proved to the Court, which date is the "onset of Insolvency"?
summary: Sections 98 and 99 of the Insolvency Regulations measure look-back periods to "the onset of Insolvency". For Part 10, Schedule 3 defines "Insolvency" as being Unable to Pay its Debts, the approval of a Voluntary Arrangement or the appointment of a Receiver or Administrative Receiver. Where inability to pay is "proved to the satisfaction of the Court" (section 50(1)(c) and (2)), the text does not say whether the onset is the date the inability began or the date of the Court's finding; section 98(c) points to the order date for one case only. For comparison, the corresponding ADGM provision (Insolvency Regulations 2015, section 259(3)) defines the onset of insolvency in a separate subsection by reference to formal events.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Foundations Regulations Schedule 3: fine row "6(6)" for failing to give a copy of an assignment; the duty and the fine are in s.6(7)
summary: Row "6(6) Person failing to provide a copy of assignment of rights - 1,500". s.6(6) only permits assignment of rights if the By-laws allow. The duty to give the Registrar a copy within 30 days, with "liable to a fine, as set out in Schedule 3", is s.6(7). Amendments No. 3 (2023) itself quotes 6(7) as the fine provision. The description in the row matches 6(7).
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Foundations Regulations s.36: since Amendments No. 1 (2019) "the Foundation's return date" is not defined; since Amendments No. 3 (2023) s.36(4)-(5) still refer to "Schedule 3 (Fines and Fees)" and to fees "prescribed in Regulations"
summary: Amendments No. 1 to the Foundations Regulations (2019) deleted the definition of the return date ("each anniversary of the date it received its Commercial Licence") from section 36(3) but kept the words "made up to the Foundation's return date"; the term is not defined elsewhere. The filing deadline, "within 6 months of the end of each financial year", does not depend on that date, and the Registrar may set another date. Amendments No. 3 (2023) moved fees to the Fees Rules (section 61) and removed fees from Schedule 3, but section 36(4) still refers to "Schedule 3 (Fines and Fees)" and section 36(5) still requires "application for registration fees ... as prescribed in Regulations".
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Foundations Regulations s.14(1)(g): UBO particulars "required by Part 16" of the Companies Regulations; that Part is 14-1 (Part 16 does not exist)
summary: Companies Regulations V8 end with Part 15. The UBO Part was renumbered from 16 to 14-1 by A2, in force 01.03.2019. The Foundations Regulations, adopted after that (26.03.2019), cite "Part 16 (Ultimate Beneficial Owners)" in s.14(1)(g). The same act cites "Part 14-1 (Ultimate Beneficial Owners)" in its application section near the end. The heading in brackets saves the meaning.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

act: AIFC Non-Profit Incorporated Organisations Regulations, V6
location: NPIO Regulations V6, Schedule 1, definition "Authorised Activities"
title: NPIO Regulations Schedule 1: "Authorised Activities" defined by s.8, which is the prohibition; the definition is in s.9
summary: The definition reads "section 8 (Authorised Activities of Incorporated Organisations)". s.8 is "Prohibition against conducting certain activities". s.9 is "Authorised Activities of Incorporated Organisations", and s.9(2) lists them. The heading in brackets saves the meaning. The NPIO Rules fine table correctly cites "9(1) Authorised Activities".
reported_to: AIFC Authority

act: AIFC website, page of the List of financial services exempt from corporate income tax and VAT
title: aifc.kz: the page of the CIT/VAT-exempt List sends readers for the 'current version' to the regulator's page of a different act — the AML list of services subject to financial monitoring
summary: The aifc.kz page "The List of financial services provided by the AIFC participants, income from which is exempt from CIT and VAT" (Joint Order No. 126/547/118 of 2020) says that the current version can be found on the regulator's website and links to orderly.myafsa.com/articles/the-list-of-financial-services-and-ancillary-services-...-subject-to-the-financial-monitoring. That address is the regulator's page of a different act: the list of services subject to financial monitoring, which aifc.kz publishes on its own page with the same link.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

act: AIFC Regulations No. 57 of 2026 on the AIFC Investment Tax Residency Programme
location: AIFC Regulations No. 57 of 2026 (6 Aug 2026), EN, Schedule, 'Tax Code'
title: ITRP Regulations (AIFC Regulations No. 57 of 2026): "Tax Code" is the repealed Code No. 120-VI in the English and Kazakh texts, and sections 29(2) and 30(2) restate rules that current law no longer contains
summary: AIFC Regulations No. 57 of 2026 on the AIFC Investment Tax Residency Programme (6 August 2026) replaced AIFC Act No. 42 of 2022 (section 3). The English and Kazakh texts of its Schedule define "Tax Code" as the Code of 25 December 2017 No. 120-VI, which was repealed on 1 January 2026. The Russian text gives only the name of the Code, without a date or number; under Article 2(5) of the Tax Code of 18 July 2025 No. 214-VIII that name now refers to the current Code, so the language versions point to different Codes. Sections 29(2) and 30(2), carried over from Act No. 42 word for word, restate rules of Article 218(2) of the 2017 Code: the investment resident provides, "along with other documents determined by the Tax Code", the AIFC Authority's confirmation letter, and the residency certificate "is issued for the year in which the fee ... was paid". Under the 2025 Code these documents are no longer in the Code: Article 224(1) leaves the procedure to the authorised body, and the list for an AIFC investment resident, including the confirmation letter, is in item 8(6) of the list of requirements to the Rules approved by Order of the Minister of Finance of 11 November 2025 No. 689. The 2025 Code and Order No. 689 do not keep the fee-year rule: Article 224(3)(3) confirms residency for the calendar year stated in the application and Article 224(4) for the past and (or) the current year. For example, an investor who pays the fee in January 2026 and asks for confirmation for 2025 would get a certificate for 2026 under section 30(2), while Article 224(4) allows 2025. Sections 29(1) and 30(1) refer to the acting tax legislation, so residency itself follows current law, but section 30(2) states a period that current law does not set.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Consolidated V3 and V4 of the Employment Regulations drop the text of section 65-1 (Whistleblowing); only the contents entry remains
summary: Version 2 of the Employment Regulations (amendments as of 22 February 2019) contains Part 10-1 with section 65-1, which extends to Employees the whistleblower protections of Part 14-2 of the Companies Regulations. The later amending instruments on the act page (No. 30 of 2019 and No. 39 of 2021) do not omit it. Yet the consolidated V3 and the current V4 list "PART 10-1: WHISTLEBLOWING" in the contents but have no text for it. The full text on the aifc.kz website goes from Part 10 to Part 11 and has no Part 10-1 and no section 65-1. The act page publishes no instrument that inserted section 65-1 in February 2019, and no instrument that omitted it. Part 14-2 of the Companies Regulations still protects any Worker directly.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Employment Regulations s.26: rest breaks of "not less than 15 hours" for a working day of more than 6 hours
summary: Section 26 of the Employment Regulations entitles an Employee whose working time on a day is more than 6 hours to rest breaks of "not less than 15 hours" in total; the breaks "may be spent away from the Employee's workstation". With the 8-hour limit in section 24 this makes a day of 23 hours of work and breaks, and more than 24 hours once working time exceeds 9 hours, so the figure is hard to apply as a break during work. The text has been the same since 2017. For comparison, the ADGM Employment Regulations (2015, 2019 and 2024), which have the same structure and the same 6-hour trigger, give rest breaks of not less than 1 hour in aggregate. The intended figure cannot be derived from the AIFC text itself.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Foreign-labour record rules (2018) put the reporting duty on the foreign employee; Article 8(3) of the Constitutional Statute, as amended in December 2019, names AIFC Participants and bodies
summary: Article 8(3) of the Constitutional Statute, as amended by Constitutional Law No. 296-VI of 30 December 2019, requires Participants and bodies of the Centre to submit information on attracted foreign nationals to the AIFC Authority "in accordance with acts of the Centre". The only implementing act we found, AIFC Rules No. 2 of 2018 (rule 2.2), puts the duty on the Foreign Employee, who may file in person or through the Employer. The two duties can coexist, but we found no act of the Centre addressed to Participants and bodies. Rule 2.2 also uses "admit" where "apply" or "submit" seems meant.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: DP Regulations 2025: section 9-2 'Right to withdraw consent' is listed and cited twice but has no text
summary: Section 9-1(5) twice refers to section 9-2: the right to withdraw consent "afforded ... under section 9-2" and the duty to inform the Data Subject "how to exercise it as set out in section 9-2". The contents list "9-2. Right to withdraw consent", but the text passes from section 9-1(12) directly to section 10. Section 9-1(5) itself says that consent may be withdrawn at any time, that withdrawing must be at least as easy as giving consent and that it does not affect earlier processing; section 9-1(9) requires procedures for recording withdrawal. The amending instrument of 1 April 2025 is not on the act page, so it cannot be established whether the instrument or the consolidation lost section 9-2.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Data Protection Regulations s.9: the lawful-basis rule is addressed to the Data Processor, while other sections treat it as the Data Controller's basis - who is bound?
summary: Section 9 of the Data Protection Regulations opens "A Data Processor must not Process Personal Data unless" one of grounds (a)-(e) applies. The grounds themselves refer to the Data Controller, and sections 9-1(1), 13(1)(c)(v) and 14(2)(c)(v) treat section 9 as the Controller's lawful basis. The Controller's duty to process lawfully also follows from section 8(1)(a). A Processor may well be meant to be bound too, so the text allows more than one reading of who is bound by section 9. For comparison, the corresponding ADGM provision (Data Protection Regulations 2015, section 2) opened without naming an addressee: "Personal Data may only be Processed if".
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: s.16-2(7) points to 'measures referred to in section 24-1(1) and 24-1(2)'; s.24-1 contains no measures
summary: Section 16-2(7): adherence by a Processor or Sub-processor to an approved certification mechanism "may demonstrate the sufficiency of the measures referred to in section 24-1(1) and 24-1(2)". Section 24-1(1) allows a certification scheme to be established; section 24-1(2) says certification does not relieve responsibility. None of them refers to any measures. The assurances and measures of processors and sub-processors are dealt with in section 16-2(1), (2) and (3).
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: DP Rules r.4.2.3(a): first notification due 'no later than 14 days start of the operations' - before or after the start is not said
summary: Rule 4.2.3(a) requires the notification of Personal Data Processing operations 'no later than 14 days start of the operations' - a word ('after' or 'before') is missing, so the deadline can be read as 14 days before the operations start or 14 days after. The neighbouring r.4.3 uses the full form 'no later than 14 days after the day the particulars change'. Text unchanged since the 2018 Rules; the notification attracts the item 3 fee (USD 1,000/500/200).
reported_to: AIFC Authority

location: Schedule 1, note under the table of fees
title: DP Rules Schedule 1: the 50% fee reduction for 1 March 2025 - 1 March 2026 appears only in a "Note", which is not part of the act
summary: Under the fees table of Schedule 1 (items 2 and 3) the 2025 consolidation adds: "Note: For the period commencing on 1 March 2025 and concluding on 1 March 2026, the fees under items 2 and 3 of the Table of fee are applied with 50% reduction." Under section 26(1)(a) of the AIFC Regulations on AIFC Acts a note is not part of the act, and under section 27 a note is merely explanatory. Rule 7.2 and the table still set the full amounts. The amending instrument of 2025 is not on the act page, so we could not see whether it contains an operative rule for the reduction. The period ended on 1 March 2026.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: Court Rules r.28.7: 'Part 23 (judgments and orders)' applies to small claims, but Part 23 is the Abridged Procedure; judgments and orders are Part 24
summary: Rule 28.7(9) lists "Part 23 (judgments and orders)" among the provisions that apply to small claims. Part 23 is "Abridged Procedure for Claims"; "Judgments and Orders" is Part 24. The words in brackets are part of the rule. The unofficial Russian translation repeats "Часть 23 (судебные решения и приказы)", while its own contents name Part 24 "Судебные решения и приказы".
reported_to: AIFC Court

title: Court Rules fix filing and service cut-off at '4pm Alma Ata time (UTC + 6)'; Kazakhstan has used UTC+5 since 1 March 2024
summary: Rule 2.12 requires any act due "on or before a particular date" to be done "by 4pm Alma Ata time (UTC + 6)", and rule 5.15 treats a document "delivered before 4pm Alma Ata time (UTC + 6) on a business day" as served that day. When the Rules were written both labels meant the same time. Since 1 March 2024 the whole of Kazakhstan uses the fifth time zone, UTC+5 (Resolution of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 20 of 19 January 2024, amending Resolution No. 1749 of 23 November 2000). Since then "Alma Ata time" and "UTC + 6" differ by one hour: 4pm UTC+6 is 3pm local time, and 4pm local time is 5pm UTC+6.
reported_to: AIFC Court

title: Court Regulations s.29(2) restates Article 13(6) of the Constitutional Statute as "shall be guided by decisions"; Article 13(6) says the Court may take into account final decisions
summary: Section 29(2) of the AIFC Court Regulations says that the Court, "as provided by Article 13(6)" of the Constitutional Statute, "shall be guided by decisions of the Court and decisions made in other common law jurisdictions". Article 13(6) is permissive and limited to final decisions: the Court "может учитывать вступившие в законную силу решения" (may take into account final decisions). Being guided is not the same as being bound, so we do not see a clear conflict, but the restatement is not exact.
reported_to: AIFC Management Council; AIFC Authority; AIFC Court

title: Court Regulations s.13: the Chief Justice appoints temporary Judges; the Statute (art. 13(3-1), from 2018) reserves appointment of judges to the President
summary: Section 13(1) of the AIFC Court Regulations lets the Chief Justice, after consulting the Governor, appoint a person as a temporary Judge "to facilitate the disposal of business in the Court"; section 13(3) treats that person "for all purposes" as a Judge. The Regulations were adopted on 5 December 2017 under Article 13(5) of the Constitutional Statute (section 2). At that time Article 13(5) left to the Council resolution on the Court "the procedure for the appointment and removal of judges and other officials of the court". Constitutional Law No. 119-VI of 22 December 2017 added Article 13(3-1): the Chairman and judges of the Centre's court are appointed and released by the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan on the recommendation of the Governor. The same law deleted the words "judges and other" from Article 13(5), so the Council resolution now sets the procedure only for officials of the court. Section 12(1) of the Regulations follows Article 13(3-1) for permanent Judges; section 13 was not aligned. As written, a person appointed under section 13 would hear cases and sign judgments as a Judge without the appointment that Article 13(3-1) requires. We found no sign that section 13 has been used: the judges named in the judgments published on court.aifc.kz since April 2019 are all among the Chief Justice and Justices listed by the Court.
reported_to: AIFC Management Council; AIFC Authority; AIFC Court

act: AIFC International Arbitration Centre Arbitration and Mediation Rules 2022
title: IAC Rules 10.7 give 'seven days' to apply to the AIFC Court on a rejected challenge; Arbitration Regulations 22(3), which parties cannot cut, give thirty
summary: IAC Rules 10.7: a decision rejecting a challenge is "without prejudice to any right a party may have to apply within seven days to the AIFC Court under the Arbitration Regulations, Article 22(3)". Article 22(3) of the Arbitration Regulations gives the challenging party "thirty days after having received notice of the decision rejecting the challenge", and Article 22(1) makes any procedure agreed by the parties subject to paragraph (3). The AIFC Court Rules (rule 27.28) also fix 30 days for this application. Because rule 10.7 is "without prejudice to any right", the 30 days are not cut, but the Rules state the wrong period. The unofficial Russian translation also says "в течение семи дней" (within seven days).
reported_to: AIFC International Arbitration Centre

act: AIFC International Arbitration Centre Arbitration and Mediation Rules 2022
title: IAC Rules: two Articles are numbered 7.4; the second refers to "Articles 7.3 and 7.4"
summary: Article 7.4 (objection that the Tribunal is exceeding the scope of its authority) is followed by a second Article 7.4 ("The Tribunal may rule on an objection referred to in Articles 7.3 and 7.4 ..."). By the word "objection" the reference is to the first 7.4, but any citation of "Article 7.4" is ambiguous. The unofficial Russian translation numbers the second one 7.5.
reported_to: AIFC International Arbitration Centre

act: AIFC International Arbitration Centre Arbitration and Mediation Rules 2022
title: IAC Rules 3.2 calculate periods in "Alma-Ata Time (UTC+6)" by default; Kazakhstan has used UTC+5 since 1 March 2024
summary: Article 3.2: "Unless the Registrar or Tribunal provide otherwise, or unless the parties agree otherwise", "any period of time is to be calculated in accordance with Alma-Ata Time (UTC+6)". Since 1 March 2024 the whole of Kazakhstan uses UTC+5 (Resolution of the Government of the Republic of Kazakhstan No. 20 of 19 January 2024). Alma-Ata local time and UTC+6 now differ by one hour, so the default end of a day differs too (midnight local time is 01:00 UTC+6). The Registrar may extend time limits (Article 3.8), which reduces the practical effect.
reported_to: AIFC International Arbitration Centre

act: AIFC International Arbitration Centre Arbitration and Mediation Rules 2022
title: IAC Rules 2022: Article 1.4 still gives 1 January 2018 as the commencement date, and the 2022 edition does not say from when its changes apply
summary: The IAC Arbitration and Mediation Rules 2022 say in Article 1.4 that they "shall come into force on 1 January 2018" and apply to arbitrations commenced on or after that date. The 2022 text was approved by the Chairman of the IAC on 19 September 2022, but it does not say from when its changes apply. Article 2.2 refers to the rules "in force at the date of the commencement of the arbitration", so the parties need that date to know which edition governs.
reported_to: AIFC International Arbitration Centre

title: Arbitration Regulations Art. 9(2): for foreign-seated arbitrations Articles 17 and 18 apply, but not Article 16 (stay of court proceedings)
summary: Article 9(2) of the AIFC Arbitration Regulations applies "Articles 17, 18, Part 3, and the Schedule" where the seat is outside the AIFC. Article 16 (what the AIFC Court must do when an action is brought in a matter that is subject to an arbitration agreement) is not listed. In the UNCITRAL Model Law (article 1(2)) the corresponding articles 8 and 9 apply whatever the place of arbitration. The AIFC Court can still stay proceedings under its general powers (section 27(2)(g) of the Court Regulations, rule 8.8 of the Court Rules), so the question is whether the Article 16 rule is meant to apply as well.
reported_to: AIFC Management Council; AIFC Authority; AIFC International Arbitration Centre

title: Recognition of arbitral awards: Article 14(4) of the Constitutional Statute and Article 45(1) of the Arbitration Regulations; the English translation of Article 14(4) is narrower than the Russian and Kazakh texts
summary: Article 14(4) of the Constitutional Statute (Russian and Kazakh texts) provides that recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards on the territory of the Centre follow the legislation of the Republic of Kazakhstan. The English translation on aifc.kz reads "Awards of arbitration courts in the Republic of Kazakhstan", which is narrower. Article 45(1) of the AIFC Arbitration Regulations provides for recognition and enforcement by the AIFC Court of an award "irrespective of the State or jurisdiction in which it was made". The structure of Article 14 supports the narrower reading; on it, the two rules overlap only for awards made in Kazakhstan outside the AIFC. We do not claim that Article 45 cannot be applied.
reported_to: AIFC Management Council; AIFC Authority; AIFC Court

act: AIFC Regulations on Damages and Remedies
title: aifc.kz page of the Regulations on Damages and Remedies sends readers for the 'current version' to the AFSA Auditor Rules
summary: Under "Effective Version" the aifc.kz page of the AIFC Regulations on Damages and Remedies states "current version can be found on Regulator's website:" and links https://orderly.myafsa.com/articles/auditorrules. That section of the AFSA rulebook is the AIFC Auditor Rules. The Regulations on Damages and Remedies (No. 17 of 2017) are not an AFSA rulebook. The same link appears on the aifc.kz page of the Auditor Rules. The only PDF offered is the 2017 text.
reported_to: AIFC Authority

title: FAR 25.1101(b)(1)(iv) refers to 25.102(d); section 25.102 has no paragraph (d)
summary: FAR 25.1101(b)(1)(iv) applies when the senior procurement executive allows an alternate domestic content test “in accordance with 25.102(d)”. Section 25.102 is a single unnumbered paragraph. The authority for the alternate domestic content test is in 25.101(d). The FAR Overhaul Part 25 text keeps the same reference at 25.601(b)(1)(iv).
reported_to: FAR Council (General Services Administration, Federal Acquisition Policy Division); Office of the Federal Register, National Archives; Department of Defense, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy

title: FAR 25.101(d)(2)(i) refers to 25.1101(b)(1)(v); paragraph 25.1101(b)(1) ends at (iv)
summary: FAR 25.101(d)(2)(i) says “See 25.1101(a)(1)(ii) or 25.1101(b)(1)(v) for use of the appropriate Alternate clause”. Paragraph 25.1101(b)(1) ends at (iv), which prescribes Alternate IV for the alternate domestic content test. The FAR Overhaul version refers to 25.601(b)(1)(v), which also ends at (iv).
reported_to: FAR Council (General Services Administration, Federal Acquisition Policy Division); Office of the Federal Register, National Archives; Department of Defense, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy

title: FAR 52.225-9(b)(3)(i) and 52.225-11(b)(4)(i): headings (A) and (B) overlap when a material is a critical item or contains critical components, but not both
summary: In both clauses, heading (A) covers “domestic construction material that is not a critical item or does not contain critical components”, and heading (B) covers material that “is a critical item or contains critical components”. When exactly one of the two conditions holds, both headings apply. The corresponding heading in FAR 25.204(b)(1) uses “and”: material that “is not a critical item and does not contain critical components”. The list of critical items at 25.105(a)(1)-(2) is reserved.
reported_to: FAR Council (General Services Administration, Federal Acquisition Policy Division); Office of the Federal Register, National Archives; Department of Defense, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy

title: FAR 25.205(c): should the minimum consideration for a postaward exception cite 25.204 directly?
summary: FAR 25.205(c) sets the minimum consideration for a postaward exception based on unreasonable price by reference to the amount “established in 25.202(a) or in accordance with agency procedures”. Paragraph 25.202(a)(3) sets no amount; it points onward to 25.204, which adds 20 percent of the cost of the foreign construction material. Clauses 52.225-9(c)(2) and 52.225-11(c)(2) state their own minimum by reference to the evaluation factor in each clause. One reading takes the reference to 25.202(a) to reach the 25.204 factor through (a)(3). The other reads 25.202(a) as naming no amount, so that the minimum comes from agency procedures or the clause.
reported_to: FAR Council (General Services Administration, Federal Acquisition Policy Division)

title: FAR 52.225-9(b)(3)(i)(A)(2): should the U.S.-manufacture condition sit on the selected offer, as in Part 25?
summary: The provisions concern construction material that is not a commercially available off-the-shelf (COTS) item and is not wholly or predominantly iron or steel, during the fallback period before January 1, 2030. FAR 25.204(b)(1)(ii) applies when the low offer does not exceed 55 percent domestic content, and treats as domestic the lowest offer that is manufactured in the United States and exceeds 55 percent domestic content. Clause 52.225-9(b)(3)(i)(A)(2) instead requires the low offer to be manufactured in the United States, and treats as domestic the lowest offer above 55 percent without that condition. Clause 52.225-11(b)(4)(i)(A)(2) follows Part 25. One reading applies 52.225-9 as written in contracts that include it. The other reads it in line with Part 25 and 52.225-11.
reported_to: FAR Council (General Services Administration, Federal Acquisition Policy Division)

location: FAR 25.106(c)(1)(ii) and (c)(2)(ii); FAR Overhaul Part 25 guide, same paragraphs
title: FAR 25.106(c)(1)(ii) and (c)(2)(ii): should the critical-item price tests name the critical calculation expressly?
summary: For end products that are critical items or contain critical components, 25.106(c)(1)(ii) and (c)(2)(ii) test the price against the low offer after addition of “the appropriate evaluation factor in accordance with paragraph (a) or (b) of this section”. Paragraph (b) gives the factors for end products that are not critical items. Paragraph (a)(1) directs use of the factors in paragraphs (b) and (c), paragraph (c)(1)(i) specifies the critical calculation, and (c)(2)(i)(B) expressly applies the factors in (c)(1). One reading takes the reference through (a) to the critical calculation. The other follows the alternative reference to (b). The FAR Overhaul Part 25 guide keeps the same references.
reported_to: FAR Council (General Services Administration, Federal Acquisition Policy Division)

title: FAR 25.202(a)(2): should the relief from a nonavailability determination state that it applies when the fallback procedures are used?
summary: FAR 25.202(a)(2) says a nonavailability determination is not required before January 1, 2030, if there is an offer for a foreign construction material that exceeds 55 percent domestic content, with a cross-reference to 25.204(b)(1)(ii) and (b)(2)(ii). Those paragraphs set the fallback procedures and their conditions. The 2022 final rule preamble says the language clarifies that a determination is not required when the fallback procedures are used. One reading applies the sentence whenever such an offer exists. The other reads it, with the cross-reference and the preamble, as limited to cases in which the fallback procedures are used.
reported_to: FAR Council (General Services Administration, Federal Acquisition Policy Division)

title: FAR 52.225-11(c)(1)(i)(H): should the justification refer to paragraph (b)(4), as the introduction does?
summary: Under 52.225-11(c)(1)(i), a contractor request to use foreign construction material “in accordance with paragraph (b)(4)” must include listed information. Item (H) asks for a detailed justification of the reason for use of foreign construction materials “cited in accordance with paragraph (b)(3)”. Paragraph (b)(3) is the list of excepted materials. Paragraph (b)(4) states the grounds on which the Contracting Officer may add material to that list. One reading takes (H) to ask for a justification under the grounds in (b)(4). The other takes it to refer to the materials on the (b)(3) list.
reported_to: FAR Council (General Services Administration, Federal Acquisition Policy Division)

act: Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (48 CFR chapter 2) and Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1
title: DFARS 225.7003-3(b)(2)(i)(D)(1): should the COTS fastener exception also list components, as the statute and clause do?
summary: DFARS 225.7003-3(b)(2)(i)(D)(1) treats commercially available off-the-shelf (COTS) fasteners as excepted when they are incorporated into “COTS end items, subsystems, or assemblies”. Clause 252.225-7009(c)(2)(i)(D)(1) and 10 U.S.C. 4863(h)(2)(D)(i) also list components. For example, a separate subcontract supplies COTS fasteners containing specialty metal for a COTS component that will enter a non-COTS end item. One reading applies the narrower list in Part 225 to that acquisition. The other reads Part 225 in line with the statute and the clause.
reported_to: Department of Defense, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy

act: Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (48 CFR chapter 2) and Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1
title: Molybdenum in 10 U.S.C. 4872(f)(1): what interim contract instructions apply while the DFARS definition is updated?
summary: Public Law 119-60, section 844(a)(1), added molybdenum to the definition of covered material in 10 U.S.C. 4872(f)(1). The DFARS definition in 225.7018-1, the definition in Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1, and clause 252.225-7961 keep the five-material list without molybdenum. DFARS case 2024-D014 already covers this amendment. One view is that the statutory prohibition applies to DoD acquisitions of molybdenum now. The other is that contract obligations follow the clause list, which does not include molybdenum, until the case is completed.
reported_to: Department of Defense, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy

act: Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (48 CFR chapter 2) and Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1
title: 10 U.S.C. 4872(c)(3)(D): how should the exception for recycled tantalum, tungsten and molybdenum be reflected in contracts?
summary: Section 844(a) of Public Law 119-60 added 4872(c)(3)(D): tantalum, tungsten, or molybdenum produced from recycled material, if the contractor demonstrates to the Secretary that the recycled material was produced outside a covered nation and melting and all further processing and manufacturing take place in the United States or in the country of a qualifying foreign government. When these conditions are met, the prohibition in 4872(a)(1) does not apply. The deviation and clause 252.225-7961 keep only the exception for recycled neodymium-iron-boron magnets. Case 2024-D014 includes this amendment. One reading lets a contractor that meets the statutory conditions rely on the exception now. The other keeps the clause restriction until the clause is amended, because the statutory exception does not by itself establish compliance with the contract.
reported_to: Department of Defense, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy

act: Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (48 CFR chapter 2) and Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1
title: 10 U.S.C. 4872(c)(3)(C): how should the exception for recycled samarium-cobalt magnets be reflected in contracts?
summary: Section 844(a) of Public Law 119-60 added samarium-cobalt magnets to the exception in 4872(c)(3)(C) for magnets manufactured from recycled material, with milling of the recycled material and sintering of the final magnet in the United States. The deviation and clause 252.225-7961 keep the exception for recycled neodymium-iron-boron magnets only. The clause also states that its restriction on samarium-cobalt magnets is in addition to any applicable specialty metals restriction. Case 2024-D014 includes this amendment. One reading lets a magnet that meets the statutory conditions fall outside the clause now. The other keeps the clause restriction until it is amended, with any specialty metals restriction applying separately.
reported_to: Department of Defense, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy

act: Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (48 CFR chapter 2) and Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1
title: 10 U.S.C. 4872(e): how should a statutory national-security waiver be reflected in clause 252.225-7961?
summary: Section 4872(e)(1) allows the Secretary to accept delivery of an end item containing covered material manufactured in a covered nation on a written determination that acceptance is necessary to the national security interests of the United States. Paragraph (e)(3) allows a waiver made under 4863(k) to be applied to these restrictions. Case 2024-D014 covers the amendment that made those waivers applicable. The procedure in the deviation and clause 252.225-7961(c) provide for a nonavailability determination and do not describe these waiver paths. One reading lets a valid waiver govern delivery without a change to the clause. The other requires the contract restriction to be modified to reflect it.
reported_to: Department of Defense, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy

act: Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (48 CFR chapter 2) and Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1
title: DFARS 225.7018-2(a)(2) and clause 252.225-7961: does “mined, refined, or separated” reach ore and feedstock stages?
summary: For contracts awarded on or after January 1, 2027, Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1, bars covered material “mined, refined, or separated in any covered country”, and clause 252.225-7961 uses the same words. The earlier clause 252.225-7052 described the restriction for each listed material, from mining or production of an ore or feedstock, including recycled material, through finished products. One reading applies the new words to the ore and feedstock stages from which the listed material is made. The other limits them to the listed covered material itself.
reported_to: Department of Defense, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy

act: Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (48 CFR chapter 2) and Class Deviation 2026-O0041, Revision 1
location: DFARS 252.225-7052 and 252.225-7961; DPCAP memorandum of October 5, 2026
title: DFARS 252.225-7052 and 252.225-7961: is there guidance on performance before an existing contract is modified?
summary: The DPCAP memorandum of October 5, 2026 directs contracting officers to incorporate 252.225-7961 and remove 252.225-7052 in existing contracts as soon as practicable, and not to request consideration when making the modification under FAR 1.107(d). Clause 7052 applies its upstream restriction to deliveries from January 1, 2027. Clause 7961 and the statute as amended by section 848 attach it to contracts awarded on or after that date. One reading keeps the 7052 text binding on performance until the modification is made. The other treats the amended statute and the directed replacement as removing the upstream restriction for contracts awarded before that date.
reported_to: Department of Defense, Defense Pricing, Contracting, and Acquisition Policy

act: Uniform Guidance, 2 CFR part 184 (Buy America preferences for infrastructure projects)
location: 2 CFR 184.6(a)(4); Build America, Buy America Act, section 70915(b)(2)(A)
title: 2 CFR 184.6(a)(4): how does the fiber optic cable standard implement the statutory requirement for input manufacturing?
summary: Section 70915(b)(2)(A) of the Build America, Buy America Act directs OMB to ensure that its standards require that each manufacturing process required for the manufacture of the construction material and its inputs occurs in the United States. For fiber optic cable, 2 CFR 184.6(a)(4) requires ribboning (where applicable), buffering, fiber stranding and jacketing in the United States. It includes the glass and optical fiber standards and excludes the standards for non-ferrous metals, plastic and polymer-based products, and other materials. The 2023 preamble explains why OMB treated the cable as a single construction material with its own standard. One reading treats the listed processes as the definition Congress delegated to OMB. The other asks whether the manufacture of polymer and other non-fiber inputs before jacketing is also required.
reported_to: Office of Management and Budget, Made in America Office

act: Uniform Guidance, 2 CFR part 184 (Buy America preferences for infrastructure projects)
location: 2 CFR 184.6(a)(8) and (b); Build America, Buy America Act, section 70915(b)(2)(A)
title: 2 CFR 184.6(a)(8): how does the engineered wood standard implement the statutory requirement for input manufacturing?
summary: Section 70915(b)(2)(A) of the Build America, Buy America Act directs OMB to ensure that its standards require that each manufacturing process required for the manufacture of the construction material and its inputs occurs in the United States. For engineered wood, 2 CFR 184.6(a)(8) covers all manufacturing processes from the initial combination of constituent materials until the wood product is in its final form. The 2023 preamble says that only the engineered wood standard applies, even though the lumber and polymer standards could otherwise apply, and explains the standard by the manufacturing processes used in the industry. One reading treats the combination of constituents as the starting point OMB chose under its delegated authority. The other asks whether the manufacture of previously manufactured lumber inputs is also required.
reported_to: Office of Management and Budget, Made in America Office

act: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 6 (Editor's Draft, 28 April 2026)
title: CSS Cascade 6: §3.5.1 says scope proximity wins regardless of specificity, while §3.1 compares specificity first
summary: §3.5.1 of the Editor's Draft says the cascade prefers the more proximate scoping root “regardless of specificity”. §3.1 lists Specificity before Scope Proximity, and the changes list records “Removed strong scope proximity” after the Working Group resolved in issue 6790 that proximity is weaker than specificity. The §3.5.1 sentence still describes the old rule; the Working Draft of 6 September 2024 has the same sentence.
reported_to: W3C CSS Working Group

act: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 6 (Editor's Draft, 28 April 2026)
title: CSS Cascade 6: an example of overlapping scopes in §3.5.1 does not follow the current definition of scoping limits
summary: The last block of example #example-463550a5 uses to ([data-scope] > *) and says both sections are part of the outer scope. Under §3.5.2 and §3.5.4 the scope end is an ordinary selector list, so both children of the outer section, a p and the inner section, are scoping limits and are out of scope. The example holds only if the scope end is matched relative to :scope, which open issue 13290 proposes; the note was sent there as a comment.
reported_to: W3C CSS Working Group

act: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 6 (Editor's Draft, 28 April 2026)
title: CSS Cascade 6: §3.6 on presentational hints points to Level 5 §6.4 Cascade Layers instead of §6.5
summary: §3.6 has no text of its own, only an issue box pointing to “CSS Cascading 5 § 6.4 Cascade Layers”. In Level 5 presentational hints are §6.5, and Level 5 moved them out of layers into their own origin (issue 6659). The other pointers of the same kind in Level 6 go to the matching Level 5 section; the Working Draft of 6 September 2024 has the same pointer in §2.6.
reported_to: W3C CSS Working Group

act: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 5 (Editor's Draft, 13 April 2026)
title: CSS Cascade 5: the Layer Ordering example gives two different orders when both media queries match
summary: Example #example-87e2d331 in §6.4.3 says that when the width query matches, layout comes first, and that when the colour-scheme query matches, theme comes first. When both match, the two sentences give different orders. The rule of §6.4.3 (layers sort by first declaration) gives layout first; only the second sentence is wrong. The 2022 snapshot of the specification (13 January 2022) has the same example.
reported_to: W3C CSS Working Group

act: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 5 (Editor's Draft, 13 April 2026)
title: CSS Cascade 5: what does revert-rule roll back in a style attribute?
summary: §7.3.6 rolls revert-rule back “as if the current style rule had not been present”. §6.1 separates declarations in a style attribute from style rules, and §7.3.6 has a sentence for the animation origin but none for the style attribute. The same question for revert-layer was settled in issue 6743 with a dedicated sentence in §7.3.5. Browsers already agree on normal declarations: the web-platform-tests case for a style attribute passes in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari with the 5px result (stable runs of 31 October 2026); no test covers !important.
reported_to: W3C CSS Working Group

act: CSS Shadow Module Level 1 (Editor's Draft, 28 April 2026)
title: CSS Shadow 1: the exportparts form “::ident : outerIdent” is rejected by the rules for parsing part mappings
summary: §5.3 defines the exportparts form ::ident : outerIdent and example #example-b11a0a88 uses ::before : preceding-text. §5.6.1 collects the leading token from code points that are not spaces or colons and returns an error when it is empty; ::before starts with a colon, so the token is empty, and §5.6.2 drops the mapping. The form defined in §5.3 can never be produced by the parser.
reported_to: W3C CSS Working Group

act: CSS Nesting Module Level 1 (Editor's Draft, 8 October 2026)
title: CSS Nesting 1: the two forms of “Example nesting Scoping” are called equivalent but set different properties
summary: In example #example-81212ace of §3.3 the nested form sets border on :scope, while the form given as “equivalent to” sets only border-block-end. The scoping examples in §3.2 use border-block-end in both forms, so border here looks like a typo.

summary: CSS Animations 1 §3 says that of several @keyframes with the same name the last one in document order wins. act: The OAuth 2.1 Authorization Framework, draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-17 (31 October 2026)
title: OAuth 2.1 draft: §4.1.3 rejects every token request without a code challenge, so, read literally, the PKCE exemption of §7.5.1.1 has no successful outcome
summary: §7.5.1.1 lets a confidential client that uses the OpenID Connect nonce skip the code challenge. The last bullet of §4.1.3 says the authorization server must reject a token request when the authorization request had no code challenge. Read literally, a client that uses the exemption receives a code but its token request must be rejected. RFC 9700 rejects only a token request that contains a code verifier, and the third bullet of §4.1.3 already covers that case. Draft-17 of 31 October 2026 rewords the bullet; the point is the same.

title: OAuth 2.1 draft: §1.5 requires https for all client URLs and leaves out the private-use redirect URIs that §8.4.3 describes
summary: §1.5 says all OAuth protocol URLs, including those of the client, must use https, with one exception for loopback redirect URIs. §8.4.3 describes private-use URI scheme redirect URIs of native apps such as com.example.app:/oauth2redirect/example-provider, and §2.3.1 tells the server how to check them. act: The OAuth 2.1 Authorization Framework, draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1-17 (31 October 2026)

summary: §6.1.1 says RFC 6750 establishes the OAuth Extensions Error Registry and points to Section 11.4 of RFC 6749 in the same sentence. The registry was established by RFC 6749 (Sections 7.2 and 11.4); RFC 6750 only registers values in it, and §11 of the draft says it does not require any IANA actions. title: AI Act, Annex VIII, Section C, point 5: the data protection impact assessment is referred to Article 26(8) instead of 26(9)
summary: Article 26(8) is about registration by deployers that are public authorities. The data protection impact assessment is in Article 26(9). The error is in all 24 versions. This has been pointed out publicly before.

title: AI Act after the Digital Omnibus: Article 49(4)(b) still lists point 9 of Annex VIII, Section B, which was deleted
summary: Article 1, point (42), of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 deleted points 7 and 9 of Annex VIII, Section B. Article 49(4)(b) still lists points 8 and 9 of Section B. This has been noted publicly before.

title: AI Act, Article 40(1): stray word in “set out in of Chapter V”
summary: Article 40(1), English version, reads with the obligations set out in of Chapter V.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: AI Act, Article 71(4): missing word in “accessible the public”

title: AI Act, Article 101(1): extra full stop before “when”
summary: The first subparagraph of Article 101(1), English version, has an extra full stop in whichever is higher., when.

title: AI Act, Article 101(1): missing word in “shall also into account”

title: AI Act, Article 111: “marked” for “market” in the title
summary: The title of Article 111, English version, reads already placed on the marked.

title: AI Act, Article 112(6): “asses” for “assess”
