reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: AI Act, Maltese version: Article 71(1) prints 6(40 for 6(4)
summary: Maltese Article 71(1) refers to Article 6(40 where Article 6(4) is meant (a typing error).
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: AI Act, German and Estonian versions: Article 49(2) calls a system high-risk although the provider has concluded it is not
summary: German and Estonian Article 49(2) call the object a high-risk system although the provider has concluded that it is not high-risk. The other versions say an AI system.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: AI Act: which event starts the 10-year period of Articles 18(1) and 22(3)(b) when placing on the market and putting into service fall on different dates?
summary: Articles 18(1) and 22(3)(b) count 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service. Where the two events happen on different dates, the text does not say which one starts the period.
reported_to: European Commission, European AI Office

title: AI Act: is a voter exposed to the output of a campaign tool whose recommended messages staff send on?
summary: Annex III, point 8(b), excludes AI systems to the output of which natural persons are not directly exposed. A campaign tool ranks voters and recommends which message each voter should receive; campaign staff then send those messages. The text does not say whether this counts as direct exposure to the output of the system, read with recital 62.
reported_to: European Commission, European AI Office

title: AI Act: which evaluation satisfies Article 82(1) when a compliant system presents only a risk to another public interest?
summary: Article 82(1) applies, having performed an evaluation under Article 79, to a compliant high-risk AI system that presents a risk, including a risk to other aspects of public interest protection. Article 79(2) requires an evaluation for risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, and Article 74(1) applies the general market surveillance framework of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020. The text does not say which evaluation satisfies Article 82(1) where the only risk is to another public interest.
reported_to: European Commission, European AI Office

location: Article 11(1), Greek version, as corrected in 2014
title: Rome II, Greek version: should Article 11(1) on negotiorum gestio refer to unjust enrichment, as the 2014 corrigendum made it?
summary: The Greek corrigendum of 31 December 2014 replaced, in Article 11(1), the words with this non-contractual obligation by with that unjust enrichment. Article 11 is about negotiorum gestio, and the original Greek wording, like the other versions, tied the connection to that obligation. The same corrigendum also corrected Article 10(1), on unjust enrichment.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome I, Croatian version: does Article 8(2) on employment contracts apply in the absence of a choice of law, as in the other versions?
summary: The other 23 versions open paragraph 2 with the absence of a choice by the parties. The Croatian opening repeats the condition of paragraph 3 and makes paragraph 2 depend on paragraph 2 itself. Croatian corrigenda 32008R0593R(04) and R(06) do not touch Article 8.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome I, Maltese version: Article 8(4) refers to paragraph 2 or 2a, and there is no paragraph 2a
summary: The other versions of the escape clause for employment contracts refer to paragraphs 2 or 3. Article 8 has no paragraph 2a.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome I, Irish version: is a large-risk insurance contract without a choice governed by the law of the consumer or of the insurer?
summary: The other versions point to the law of the country where the insurer has his habitual residence. The Irish text names the consumer, a party that a large-risk insurance contract does not have.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome I, Danish version: Article 7(3) refers to paragraph 3 instead of Article 3, so the paragraph refers to itself
summary: The other versions say that the parties may choose one of the listed laws in accordance with Article 3 (freedom of choice). The Danish text says in accordance with paragraph 3, the paragraph in which the words stand.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome I, Latvian version: does Article 11(1) on formal validity cover persons in the same country, as in the other versions?
summary: The other versions cover in paragraph 1 a contract between persons in the same country and in paragraph 2 persons in different countries. In the Latvian text both paragraphs cover persons in different countries.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome II, Croatian version: Articles 5(1) and 9 refer to Article 42(2), and Rome II has 32 articles
summary: The other versions of Article 5(1) (product liability) and Article 9 (industrial action) begin without prejudice to Article 4(2), the rule on common habitual residence. The Croatian text refers to Article 42(2). There is no Croatian corrigendum to Rome II.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome I, Croatian and Dutch versions: does the escape clause for employment contracts set the same test as the other versions?
summary: The other versions ask whether the contract is more closely connected with another country. The Croatian text asks for the closest connection; the Dutch text asks for a manifestly closer connection, and no other version has manifestly in this paragraph.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

location: Article 7(2), second subparagraph, Latvian and Estonian versions
title: Rome I, Latvian and Estonian versions: does the escape clause for large-risk insurance require a clear and manifest closer connection?
summary: The other versions require that it is clear from all the circumstances that the contract is manifestly more closely connected with another country. The Latvian text has no word for clear or manifestly; the Estonian text keeps clearly but not manifestly.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

location: Article 7(3), points (a) and (c), Slovak, Dutch, Finnish, Swedish, Estonian and Slovenian versions
title: Rome I, six versions: does Article 7(3) limit the choice for mass risks to the law of a Member State?
summary: In points (a) and (c) of Article 7(3) most versions limit the choice for mass-risk insurance to the law of a Member State. The Slovak, Dutch and Finnish texts of point (a) and the Swedish, Estonian and Slovenian texts of point (c) speak of a country or state.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

location: Article 4(1)(h), Lithuanian, Greek, Maltese, Hungarian and Danish versions
title: Rome I, five versions: are multilateral trading systems in Article 4(1)(h) defined by non-discretionary rules?
summary: Article 4(1)(h) covers contracts in a multilateral system that brings together interests in financial instruments in accordance with non-discretionary rules. The Lithuanian, Greek, Maltese and Hungarian texts say non-discriminatory; the Danish text says mandatory.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

act: Regulation (EC) No 593/2008 (Rome I) and Regulation (EC) No 864/2007 (Rome II)
location: Article 16 of Rome I and Article 20 of Rome II, Danish, Italian and Romanian versions
title: Rome I and Rome II, Danish, Italian and Romanian versions: does the rule on multiple liability require joint and several liability?
summary: Most versions apply the rule to several debtors liable for the same claim. The Danish and Italian texts of both Regulations, and the Romanian text of Rome I, say jointly and severally liable. The Romanian text of Rome II says liable together.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome II, Bulgarian and Slovenian versions: does Article 6(3)(b) set the same conditions as the other versions?
summary: Article 6(3)(b) lets the claimant rely on the law of the court where the market is affected in more than one country, if the market in that Member State is directly and substantially affected. The Bulgarian text says more than one Member State; the Slovenian text says directly or substantially.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome II, Croatian version: does Article 4(2) apply to the person claimed to be liable or only to a person whose liability is established?
summary: The other versions apply the common habitual residence rule to the person claimed to be liable. The Croatian text speaks of the person whose liability has been established.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome II, Croatian and Slovenian versions: must all the parties pursue a commercial activity for a choice under Article 14(1)(b)?
summary: The other versions allow a freely negotiated choice before the event where all the parties pursue a commercial activity. The Croatian and Slovenian texts say both parties.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome II, Dutch and Romanian versions: does Article 23 define habitual residence in the same way as the other versions?
summary: In the second subparagraph of Article 23(1) the Dutch text names a subsidiary, a branch or another establishment where the other versions name a branch, an agency or any other establishment. In Article 23(2) the Romanian text replaces a natural person acting in the course of his or her business activity with activity during working hours.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

location: Article 15, points (d) and (h), Romanian and Lithuanian versions
title: Rome II, Romanian and Lithuanian versions: does Article 15 describe the same matters as the other versions?
summary: In Article 15(d) the Romanian text speaks of protective measures where the other versions speak of the measures a court may take to prevent or stop injury or damage. In Article 15(h) the Lithuanian text names acquisitive prescription, which concerns property, beside the limitation of actions.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome II, Bulgarian version: does Article 22(2) cover the same acts as the other versions?
summary: The other versions cover acts intended to have legal effect. The Bulgarian text covers unilateral declarations of will with legal effects.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome II, Hungarian and Danish versions: does the review clause ask for more than the other versions?
summary: The Hungarian and Danish texts of Article 30(1) add a sentence that the other versions do not have: the report shall in particular examine non-contractual obligations arising out of traffic accidents and violations of privacy and rights relating to personality, including defamation.
reported_to: Council of the European Union, General Secretariat, Directorate for Quality of Legislation; European Parliament, Directorate for Legislative Acts

title: Rome I: which Member State prevails when two Member States impose conflicting compulsory insurance on the same risk?
summary: Point (a) of Article 7(4) gives priority to the law of the Member State imposing the obligation to take out insurance, and point (b) lets each such State require the contract to be governed by its law. The two points do not say which of two such States prevails when their rules conflict.
reported_to: European Commission, Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers

title: Rome I: where is a service supplied at a distance, for Article 6(4)(a)?
summary: Article 6(4)(a) takes out of the consumer rules services to be supplied to the consumer exclusively in a country other than that of his habitual residence. For a service supplied at a distance, for example online advice used by the consumer at home, the text does not say where the service is supplied.
reported_to: European Commission, Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers

title: Rome II: at what time is foreseeability assessed under Article 5(1), second subparagraph?
summary: The law of the habitual residence of the person claimed to be liable applies if that person could not reasonably foresee the marketing of the product. The text does not say whether foreseeability is assessed when the product was put on the market, when it was marketed in that country, or when the damage occurred.
reported_to: European Commission, Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers

title: Rome II: which event must a choice of law follow under Article 14(1)(a) when several events give rise to the damage?
summary: Article 14(1)(a) allows a choice by an agreement entered into after the event giving rise to the damage. Where several events give rise to the damage, for example a first act in one country and a final act in another, and the parties are not all pursuing a commercial activity, the text does not say which event the agreement must follow.
reported_to: European Commission, Directorate-General for Justice and Consumers

location: Commission statements published with the Regulation
title: Rome II on EUR-Lex: the XHTML text lacks two of the three Commission statements printed in the Official Journal
summary: The Official Journal prints three Commission statements after Rome II: on the review clause, on road accidents and on the treatment of foreign law. The English and French PDFs contain all three. The XHTML manifestations in Cellar contain only the statement on the review clause in 23 languages; the Croatian XHTML contains all three.
reported_to: Publications Office of the European Union

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 9.1: the rewritten rules do not give the same result as LB9 and LB10
summary: Section 9.1 says the rules from LB11 on can be rewritten so that “the overall result of the algorithm is unchanged”: replace LB10 by “× CM” and add a CM copy of every rule with AL on its left side. Applied literally, the rewrite differs from Section 6.1 in three cases: a space before a combining mark (no break instead of the LB18 break), ZWJ, which LB9 treats like CM but Section 9.1 does not mention, and AL-to-CM copies that also match marks attached to other bases. On 1,099 of the 19,346 lines of LineBreakTest.txt, 58 lines give a different result.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5.1 class AL: format characters listed as AL are Line_Break=NU in the data
summary: The class AL description lists U+0600..U+0604, U+06DD and U+110BD among the format characters of class AL. LineBreak.txt 18.0.0 gives them Line_Break=NU since Unicode 15.1 (UTC action item 176-A81), and the NU description does not mention them. The table was not updated; revision 55 has the same table.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 10 Table 4: rows LB12a and LB12b do not match Section 6 or the test rules
summary: Table 4 numbers the test rules “LB12a | 12.0 | GL ×” and “LB12b | 12.1 | [^SP, BA, HY] × GL”. Section 6 has no rule LB12b: it has LB12, “GL ×”, and LB12a, “[^SP HY HH] × GL”, and the Modifications section records that Unicode 18.0 removed BA from LB12a. Both rows are one rule name off, and the formula of row 12.1 predates both recent changes of LB12a.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

location: Section 5.1, class HL, against rule LB21a
title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5.1 class HL: “a hyphen is any character of class HY or class BA” disagrees with LB21a
summary: The class HL description says that a hyphen between a Hebrew letter and non-Hebrew text is any character of class HY or BA. Rule LB21a covers HY and HH, and the class BA description says EN DASH and FIGURE DASH do not participate in LB21a. In 18.0 EN DASH moved to BA, so the difference now applies to a common character.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #29 rev. 49, Section 4.2.6: modifier symbols are said not to be ALetter, but 58 of them are
summary: Section 4.2.6 says that modifier symbols (General_Category Sk) are not in the ALetter class and so cause word breaks by default. WordBreakProperty.txt 18.0.0 gives Word_Break=ALetter to 58 Sk code points, and Table 3 of the same annex lists them by name in the ALetter row.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

location: Section 10, example of test rule numbering
title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 10: the example “13.01) [^NU] × CL” does not match LB13 or the test rules
summary: The numbering example in Section 10 gives “13.01) [^NU] × CL” and “13.02) × EX”. LB13 has no condition on the preceding class, and the test rules number the parts “13.01) × EX” and “13.02) × CL”. The example swaps the numbers and adds a condition that no rule has; revision 55 has the same example.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5.1 class XX: unassigned code points outside CJK blocks are not all XX
summary: The class XX description includes all unassigned code points that are not within a CJK block. The PR description in the same section puts unassigned code points of the Currency Symbols block in PR, and LineBreak.txt 18.0.0 gives most unassigned code points in U+1F000..U+1FAFF and U+1FC00..U+1FFFD the default ID.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5: LB21a is listed among rules that use East_Asian_Width, General_Category and Extended_Pictographic
summary: Section 5 lists the rules that use tailorable East_Asian_Width, General_Category and Extended_Pictographic values: LB15a, LB15b, LB19, LB19a, LB21a, LB30 and LB30b. LB21a, “HL (HY | HH) × [^HL]”, uses only line break classes.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

location: file header, against the data for U+1F80C..U+1F8FF
title: LineBreak.txt 18.0.0: do the 85 unassigned code points in Supplemental Arrows-C default to ID, as the header says, or XX, as the data says?
summary: The header of LineBreak.txt says all unassigned code points in U+1F000..U+1FAFF default to ID. In the data, 85 unassigned code points in Supplemental Arrows-C (U+1F80C..U+1F80F up to U+1F8D9..U+1F8FF) are XX, and LineBreakTest.txt uses U+1F8FF as XX.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5.1 B2: is the Spanish parenthetical em dash a default behaviour or a tailoring?
summary: The B2 description says that in Spanish the dashes around a parenthetical should not be broken from the contained text; one paragraph earlier it says line breaks can occur before and after an EM DASH. The rules follow the first sentence: LB17 covers only B2 SP* × B2, and LineBreakTest.txt expects breaks between EM DASH and a following or preceding letter. The description does not say that the Spanish convention needs tailoring, and Section 8 does not mention it.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 9.2: does Legacy-CM intentionally keep the LB8 break inside ZW SP CM?
summary: Legacy-CM changes a space that is the base of a combining mark to ID only in rules following LB8. For ZERO WIDTH SPACE, SPACE and a combining mark, LB8 gives a break before the mark before the tailoring applies, so the break falls inside SP CM*, which Section 9.2 describes as an indivisible cluster under the earlier practice.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5.1 GL: should the description name the HY and HH exceptions of LB12a?
summary: The GL description names SP and ZW as what can override the no-break prohibition. LB12a also allows a break before GL after HY and HH, which the HH description explains as widespread practice.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5.1 EX: should the exception list for EX include PR?
summary: The EX description says these characters behave like closing characters except in relation to PO and NS. LB25 keeps CL and CP before PR in numeric context but not EX, so EX also differs in relation to PR.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5.1 SY: is “except in front of digits” limited to numbers?
summary: The SY description says there is a break opportunity after a solidus except in front of digits. LB25 keeps SY × NU only after digits, so after a letter a solidus followed by a number allows a break.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5.1 BA: do EN DASH and FIGURE DASH “not participate” in LB12a, or are they outside its exceptions?
summary: The BA description says these dashes do not participate in rule LB12a, so the no-break space after them stays non-breaking. After the 18.0 change LB12a is the rule that keeps it non-breaking; the outcome is right, but the wording reads as if LB12a did not apply.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #29 rev. 49, Section 4.2.1: should the text note that U+058A is ALetter and U+30A0 is Katakana by default?
summary: Section 4.2.1 says hyphens are better kept out of the default word definition and names U+058A ARMENIAN HYPHEN and U+30A0 KATAKANA-HIRAGANA DOUBLE HYPHEN. Table 3 puts U+058A in ALetter and U+30A0 in Katakana, so by default they do not break words between letters of those classes.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #29 rev. 49, Section 4.3: how is the union and intersection in the Basic Name Validation set grouped?
summary: The set “[ \p{name=/COMMA/}\p{name=/FULL STOP/}&\p{p} …” mixes union and intersection without brackets. UTS #18 does not fix one precedence and recommends brackets.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

location: Section 7, example of test rule numbering
title: UAX #29 rev. 49, Section 7: the numbering example “21.01) × $BA, 21.02) × $HY” is a line-breaking rule
summary: The example of hundredths numbering in Section 7 comes from line breaking: UAX #29 has no rule 21 and no classes BA or HY, and the segmentation test rules have no such lines. Revision 47 has the same example.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5.1: classes are said to be listed alphabetically, but HL comes after ID
summary: Section 5.1 says line breaking classes are listed alphabetically; the headings run HH, HY, ID, HL, IN.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #14 rev. 57, Section 5.1 QU and HH: misspelt “Initial_Punctation”, “Final_Punctation” and “word-initally”
summary: The QU description names the General_Category values “Initial_Punctation” and “Final_Punctation”; PropertyValueAliases.txt has Initial_Punctuation and Final_Punctuation. The HH description says “word-initally”.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

title: UAX #29 rev. 49, Section 5.1 Table 4: the name of U+1CBF is misprinted
summary: Table 4 names U+1CBF “GEORGIAN LETTER MTAVRULI CAPITAL LABIAL SIGN”; UnicodeData.txt 18.0.0 names it “GEORGIAN MTAVRULI CAPITAL LETTER LABIAL SIGN”. The range and the Sentence_Break result are not affected.
reported_to: Unicode Consortium

act: Payroll Deductions Online Calculator (PDOC), Canada Revenue Agency
location: Result for a pay dated 1 January or 1 July, when a new T4127 edition takes effect
title: PDOC: when a new edition starts, time zones east of Eastern time get the amounts of the previous day
summary: PDOC says that the date the employee is paid decides the tax rates and the CPP and EI figures, and that the July 2026 changes apply to a date paid of July 1, 2026 or later. On 23 October 2026 we ran the public calculator many times with the same entries and changed only the time zone of the browser (automated Google Chrome 155). On the day each new edition we tried took effect (1 July 2025, 1 January 2026 and 1 July 2026) the result screen showed the selected date, but in Atlantic (Halifax) and Newfoundland (St. John's) time PDOC used the amounts of the previous day. Labrador time (Goose Bay), tried on 1 July 2026, behaved the same. Toronto and Vancouver time got the new amounts. The days before and after gave the same result in every time zone. Examples, monthly pay of 4,000.00 CAD: British Columbia, 1 July 2026: provincial tax 132.21 CAD instead of 160.43 CAD. Ontario, 1 January 2026, TD1 amounts as PDOC fills them in: PDOC filled in the 2025 amounts (16,129 and 12,747 instead of 16,452 and 12,989) and showed federal tax 314.59 instead of 310.53, provincial tax 171.40 instead of 170.40 and EI 65.60 instead of 65.20. Newfoundland and Labrador, 1 July 2026: PDOC filled in 11,188 instead of 15,000 as the provincial TD1 amount (provincial tax 255.95 instead of 228.31). The PDF of the result made in Halifax time shows a date one day earlier than the screen. The form sends the date as the local midnight of the computer; we cannot see the server, so we do not know the cause. We did not check what employers actually withheld.
reported_to: Canada Revenue Agency

Article 3 No. 16 of the draft Annual Tax Act 2026 replaces § 50b and the reference disappears. The draft is not yet law.
reported_to: Federal Ministry of Finance (Bundesministerium der Finanzen); Finance Committee of the German Bundestag (Finanzausschuss)

location: Gloas fork logic (upgrade) and beacon chain (slot processing, attestation flags)
title: Gloas: the payload availability bit of the fork slot is never cleared
summary: The Gloas upgrade sets every bit of the payload availability vector to 1. After that, the processing of each slot clears the bit of the next slot. The bit of the fork slot would be cleared while the last Fulu slot is processed, but that slot runs under the Fulu rules, before the upgrade, so the bit stays 1 even when the payload of the fork block is never revealed. Attestation rewards read this bit to decide whether a vote matches the payload status. The case differs from issue 5661, where the last Fulu slot is empty and the bit belongs to a Fulu slot.
reported_to: Ethereum consensus specifications maintainers

location: Gloas fork choice, honest validator guide and networking (bid gossip)
title: Gloas fork choice and honest validator rules do not cover Fulu blocks and Fulu store entries at the fork
summary: Issue 5096 and the open pull request 5125 cover one place where Gloas fork choice reads the bid field of a Fulu parent block. The text has further places of this kind. The finalized and safe execution block hashes for the execution layer are read from the bid field of blocks that stay Fulu blocks for at least two epochs after the fork. Bid gossip ignores every bid for the fork slot, because only envelopes fill the list of known payloads and the last Fulu payload never arrives in an envelope. Fork choice gives a Fulu head only an EMPTY child, since a Fulu block never has an envelope, so the honest validator guide tells the proposer of the initial Gloas block to use the parent hash of the last Fulu payload, while the state transition requires the hash of that payload itself. The fork-choice store has no conversion at the fork, although the types of block timeliness and latest messages change in Gloas.
reported_to: Ethereum consensus specifications maintainers

location: Gloas honest builder guide (bid signature) against the beacon chain (bid verification)
title: Gloas: a builder bid for the fork slot is signed with the Fulu fork version and fails verification
summary: The honest builder guide signs a bid with the domain of the state the builder works with, and the steps before it take that state from the head of the chain. For a bid for the fork slot the head is the last Fulu block, so the domain uses the Fulu fork version, although the epoch passed in is the Gloas fork epoch. The block that includes the bid is processed on the upgraded state, where verification uses the Gloas fork version, so the signature does not verify and the block is rejected. Proposer preferences (issues 5656 and 5665) and inclusion lists (pull request 5721) had the same problem and were fixed by taking the version from the epoch; bids were not changed. Bid gossip also ignores bids for the fork slot today (issue 5795), so the problem shows once that is fixed, or for bids that reach the proposer another way.
reported_to: Ethereum consensus specifications maintainers

location: Gloas and Fulu networking: executable gossip checks
title: Executable gossip checks take the signature domain from the head state, so the opening block of a fork fails the proposer signature check
summary: The executable block gossip check in Gloas takes the state of the current head and computes the proposer signature domain from it. When the opening block of a fork arrives, the head is still the last block of the previous fork, and the domain takes the previous fork version from that state. A valid signature does not verify, and the block is rejected as having an invalid proposer signature. The same pattern is in the Gloas checks for aggregates, payload attestations and attestations, and in the Fulu checks for blocks and data column sidecars. Clients do not follow this text literally, since Fulu blocks propagated, but the next fork will copy it, and test generators that run these functions across a fork will reject valid messages.
reported_to: Ethereum consensus specifications maintainers

location: Gloas honest builder guide (onboarding note) against the Electra and Gloas beacon chain
title: Gloas: the builder onboarding note describes a deposit window that is empty unless the deposit queue has a backlog
summary: The honest builder guide says a builder can be onboarded at the fork with a deposit made late enough to be still pending at the fork, but early enough that its slot is finalized, so that the builder is active. Without a backlog in the pending deposit queue no slot meets both conditions: Fulu applies every pending deposit up to the finalized slot, and a builder is active only if its deposit epoch is before the finalized epoch. A deposit that is early enough is applied by Fulu as a validator with a 0xB0 credential, which is not an execution withdrawal credential, so the validator never gets withdrawals. A deposit that is late enough becomes a builder that is not active at the fork. The activation note of the same guide is correct as a condition.
reported_to: Ethereum consensus specifications maintainers

location: Gloas and Fulu networking: data column request and response
title: Gloas networking: the data column request protocols are not updated for the new data column sidecar
summary: Gloas removes the signed block header, the KZG commitments and the inclusion proof from DataColumnSidecar and adds the slot and the beacon block root. The Gloas request and response section updates the block request protocols with a Gloas row, but says nothing about DataColumnSidecarsByRange and DataColumnSidecarsByRoot, which stay as defined in Fulu. Their context epoch is read from the signed block header, their type table maps every epoch from the Fulu fork on to the Fulu sidecar, and the reader is told to check the inclusion proof, which a Gloas sidecar does not have.
reported_to: Ethereum consensus specifications maintainers

location: EIP-7732, Fork transition, against Gloas fork logic
title: EIP-7732: the fork onboarding text still excludes keys of existing validators
summary: EIP-7732 says that at the fork, pending deposits with the builder withdrawal prefix are converted to builders only if their public key does not belong to an existing or pending validator. Pull request 5736 in the consensus specifications, merged on 26 October 2026, changed the onboarding function on purpose: a valid builder deposit registers or tops up a builder even if a validator uses the same key, and a builder deposit for an existing builder tops it up regardless of signature. For a key that already belongs to a validator, the EIP now says the opposite of the specification.
reported_to: EIP editors

location: Fetch, determine the same-site mode, steps 2 and 3
title: Fetch: the Lax exception for cross-site navigations cannot be reached
summary: The check for a cross-site navigation initiator runs before the check for a top-level GET document. A cross-site link therefore never reaches the step meant for it, and that step catches same-site navigations instead. By the text, a Lax cookie is not sent on a cross-site link and a Strict cookie is not sent on a same-origin link.
reported_to: Fetch Standard editors

location: Fetch, determine the same-site mode, step 2, with the HTML navigate algorithm
title: Fetch: a browser UI navigation counts as cross-site
summary: HTML gives a navigation started from the browser UI a new opaque initiator origin and passes it to the request as the top-level navigation initiator origin. An opaque origin is not same site with any other origin, so the step for a cross-site initiator applies to typed addresses as well.
reported_to: Fetch Standard editors

location: Fetch, determine the same-site mode, steps 4 to 6
title: Fetch: cross-site subresources and redirected POST requests get the highest same-site mode
summary: No step compares a request with its client. The ancestor check looks at parents only, so a first request from a top-level page on a to b reaches the last step. The redirect check skips a hop when the origin of the request is same site with the URL before it, so a form POST from a to a that redirects to b reaches the last step too.
reported_to: Fetch Standard editors

title: Fetch: the response to a top-level navigation cannot set an ordinary cookie
summary: Set-Cookie processing allows Strict, Lax and unset cookies only when the mode is the highest one. A top-level GET navigation never gets that mode, so by the text its response cannot store these cookies. RFC 6265bis notes that top-level navigations can create a cookie with any SameSite value.
reported_to: Fetch Standard editors

location: Fetch, determine the same-site mode, step 1
title: Fetch: the same-site algorithm states that every request is GET or POST
summary: The first step of the algorithm states as an invariant that the method is GET or POST, but the algorithm also runs for every other method. By the Infra Standard such a false statement is an error of the document with no effect on implementations, and the remaining steps already give the right result for same-origin requests.
reported_to: Fetch Standard editors

location: Fetch, Set-Cookie processing, with layered-cookies, Requirements Specific to Browser User Agents
title: Fetch: nothing removes expired cookies unless a Set-Cookie response is processed
summary: layered-cookies leaves the removal of expired cookies in browsers to Fetch and other callers, and its retrieval steps have no expiry condition. Fetch calls the garbage collection steps only while processing Set-Cookie. If no such response is processed after a cookie expires, the steps return that cookie. The Fetch review of the integration already mentioned clearing cookies periodically, but the list of remaining pieces does not.
reported_to: Fetch Standard editors

location: layered-cookies, Parse a Cookie, loop over attributes
title: layered-cookies: Max-Age loses to a later Expires
summary: The draft says Max-Age has precedence over Expires. The variable that records a Max-Age is created inside the loop over attributes, so it is false again for every attribute and a later Expires overwrites the value.
reported_to: IETF HTTP Working Group, cookie draft editors

title: layered-cookies: the failed date check tests the wrong variable
summary: After parsing the date of an Expires attribute, the step that should skip a failed parse tests the attribute value and not the parse result. A failed date therefore goes on to the later steps as if it were a time.
reported_to: IETF HTTP Working Group, cookie draft editors

title: layered-cookies: the cap on Expires assigns a number of days to a time
summary: The cookie age limit is a number of days. When an Expires date is too far ahead, the step sets the expiry time to that limit and not to the current time plus the limit, as the comparison just before it does.
reported_to: IETF HTTP Working Group, cookie draft editors

location: layered-cookies, Parse a Cookie, SameSite, against RFC 6265bis-22 section 5.6.7
title: layered-cookies and RFC 6265bis: a last unknown SameSite value
summary: layered-cookies keeps an earlier SameSite value when the last one is unknown. RFC 6265bis-22, which it says it replaces, resets to the default. The working group has said that handling may vary per attribute, so whether this change is meant is a question for the editors. Existing web-platform-tests follow 6265bis.
reported_to: IETF HTTP Working Group, cookie draft editors

location: layered-cookies, Parse a Cookie, Path, against RFC 6265bis-22 section 5.6.4
title: layered-cookies and RFC 6265bis: a last Path without a leading slash
summary: layered-cookies keeps an earlier valid Path when the last one does not start with a slash. RFC 6265bis-22 uses the default path. Whether this change is meant is a question for the editors.
reported_to: IETF HTTP Working Group, cookie draft editors

location: layered-cookies, Parse a Cookie, Domain, against RFC 6265bis-22 section 5.7
title: layered-cookies and RFC 6265bis: an empty Domain attribute
summary: layered-cookies passes an empty Domain value to the host parser, which fails, and the cookie is rejected. RFC 6265bis-22 treats an empty value as a host-only cookie. Whether this change is meant is a question for the editors.
reported_to: IETF HTTP Working Group, cookie draft editors

title: layered-cookies: cookies are sorted by the number of path segments, not by path length
summary: Retrieve Cookies sorts by the size of the path, which is its number of segments. RFC 6265bis-22 sorts by length. The root path and a one-segment path have the same size, so creation time decides between them. An existing web-platform-test expects the longer path first.
reported_to: IETF HTTP Working Group, cookie draft editors

issuer: ETSI Technical Committee on Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures
title: ETSI TS 119 472-2: the ban on unsigned requests names a value OpenID4VP does not define
summary: OIDFVP-HAIP-API-03 bars the exchange protocol value "openid4vp-1-unsigned". OpenID4VP 1.0 defines "openid4vp-v1-unsigned". The value in the ban is not one that OpenID4VP defines, so the ban does not name the value in use. The text is the same in V1.2.1 and V1.3.1.
reported_to: ETSI TC ESI secretariat

issuer: ETSI Technical Committee on Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures
title: ETSI TS 119 472-2: the RequestInfo key is spelled differently in the CDDL and in the requirements
summary: The RequestInfo CDDL uses the key "eUWrprc". ISO/IEC 18013-REQ-06 to REQ-08 of the same clause use "euWrprc". CBOR map keys are case sensitive. Annex XII to Regulation (EU) 2026/1731 already uses "euWrprc" in its replacement CDDL, while the TS still has the other spelling in V1.2.1 and V1.3.1.
reported_to: ETSI TC ESI secretariat

issuer: ETSI Technical Committee on Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures
title: ETSI TS 119 472-2: RO-07 cites the wrong clause of TS 119 475 for srvDescription
summary: OIDFVP-HAIP-COMMON-REQ-RO-07 places srvDescription in clause B.2.2 of TS 119 475. That member is in clause B.2.1, and B.2.2 is the class LegalEntity. The CDDL for ISO/IEC 18013-REQ-11 in the same TS already cites B.2.1. Annex XII to Regulation (EU) 2026/1731 makes RO-07 void, while the TS keeps it.
reported_to: ETSI TC ESI secretariat

issuer: ETSI Technical Committee on Electronic Signatures and Trust Infrastructures
title: ETSI TS 119 472-2: VC-03 cites an example of RFC 9901 for Compact Serialization
summary: EAAP-SD-JWT VC-03 cites clause 5.2 of RFC 9901 for Compact Serialization. That clause is a non-normative presentation example. The format is specified in clause 4.
reported_to: ETSI TC ESI secretariat

location: EIP-7928, Gas Validation Before State Access, against the execution specification
title: EIP-7928: the text does not say that a static-context halt comes before pre-state validation
summary: EIP-7928 says that once pre-state validation passes, the target is accessed and included in the block access list. It does not mention a static context. Take a call with value inside a static frame, with enough gas: pre-state validation passes, so by the text the target goes in the list. The execution specification halts such a call before any gas check, and its test requires the target to stay out of the list. The other state-accessing instructions that a static frame does not allow follow the same order.
reported_to: EIP editors

act: EIP-8038: State-Access Gas Cost Update (commit dc5d5fa)
location: EIP-8038, Interaction with EIP-7928, and the pre-state validation table of EIP-7928
title: EIP-8038 and EIP-7928: the pre-state gas of contract creation is left open
summary: The pre-state validation table of EIP-7928 lists costs in addition to the base cost of the instruction and uses the older gas constant for contract creation. EIP-8038 replaces that constant with an access charge, which is also the base cost, plus a separate state gas charge, and its section on EIP-7928 does not mention the table. Read together, the two leave the pre-state amount open: a reader can add the access charge twice, or can add the state gas charge. The execution specification charges the access charge once, together with memory expansion and the init code cost. In pull request 12418, closed in October 2026, an author of EIP-7928 wrote that it would not depend on EIP-8038, so the mapping belongs in EIP-8038.
reported_to: EIP editors

act: EIP-7708: ETH Transfers Emit a Log (commit dc5d5fa)
location: EIP-7708, Specification, against its Test Cases and the execution specification
title: EIP-7708: the transfer log rules do not cover contract-creation transactions and failed frames
summary: The list in EIP-7708 covers a value transaction to a different account and the two creation instructions. It does not name a transaction with an empty recipient field, and the execution specification emits the log for it. The Specification section also does not say what happens to the log when a frame fails; only the Test Cases section lists reverts and rolled-back inner calls among the cases with no log. The execution specification drops the log with the failed frame or an enclosing one, and a creation that fails on an address collision emits no log, because the check comes before the transfer.
reported_to: EIP editors
